title: What Came Back Home
logline: A woman returns to the village she grew up in after years of work abroad, naming places before they come into view, and finds that some of what she remembers is no longer there to be seen.

object.note: Object 5 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject.

thread_in.thread: From faces glimpsed and let go to a place long remembered: a woman returning after years of work abroad, the other side of the choice left open in 'Not Yet Decided'.

thread_out.thread: Memory's long echo becomes a literal one: a temple bell struck once at dawn, its sound fading slowly across the valley.

requirements: A family with a member returning from long-term work abroad, willing to be filmed
Access to both the journey and the home over enough time to observe real adjustment
Careful, ongoing consent from the whole family, including any children

suggestions.name: A rural village in the North Western or North Central Province
suggestions.why: Regions with a long history of overseas labour migration and return.
suggestions.verify: A specific family and their willingness to be filmed over time are unconfirmed.

lesson.in_simple_terms: Remembering a place and seeing it again are two different things: the remembered village is something that has already gone, while the village in front of you is what stands there now. Coming home is partly the mind meeting its own past.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: සිහියේ ඇති ගම සහ දැන් ඇස් ඉදිරියේ ඇති ගම එකක් නොවේ; මතකය අල්ලාගෙන සිටින්නේ දැන් නැති වී ගිය දෙයකි.
lesson.the_teaching: The Abhidhamma teaches that the five senses meet only what is present, while the mind-door can take objects from the past, the present and the future, as well as names and concepts (C036). Margaya's example is a visit to a great stupa: seeing it is an eye-door process, and remembering it later at home is a mind-door process whose object is something already seen that has ceased and no longer exists (C047). The name of a place is a third kind of object again, a concept (paññatti), and Pradeepika describes recognising what something is as a later mind-door step that takes its name (C047, C046).
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: On the road home the returnee names places before they come into view and corrects the names when they don't match, so the gap between memory and the present is spoken aloud rather than explained. The family's own account of what has changed, and the quiet days of adjustment that follow, let the viewer watch the two villages, remembered and real, slowly come apart.

key_terms.en: mental object; what is taken through the mind door
concept or name, e.g. the name of a place

lesson.caution: This does not say the past is unreal or that dwelling on memories is unhealthy: the texts treat remembered things as real things that have ceased, and they only describe what remembering is.
lesson.builds_on: The three-wheeler stand showed the mind turning toward what is in front of it; this film follows the sixth door, where the mind turns toward what is no longer there.
